activity.title: I just concluded my summer at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory , where I researched how satellite megaconstellations could use onboard vision-language models to detect & triage natural disasters, and coordinate follow-up observations across multiple satellites, with no ground-in-the-loop. As part of the FAME AI group, I combined edge-deployable VLMs such as Gemma with graph-based orchestration, allowing models on different satellites to pass context and coordinate decisions as a multi-agent system. I began by benchmarking existing VLMs and fine-tuning them for disaster-detection tasks. I then built an orchestration harness that carried observations from detection through triage and follow-up planning. I tested the system using a time-series simulation of the core coordination loop across satellites under the hardware constraints of space systems. One highlight was meeting with Liquid AI and other commercial partners to discuss edge intelligence. Those conversations pushed me to communicate the system’s capabilities and limitations clearly and gave me a broader view of how the research connects across academic and commercial settings. I also enjoyed working alongside other interns exploring complementary approaches to natural-disaster detection, which showed me how many technical disciplines contribute to the same operational problem. I’m especially grateful to my mentors Steve, Jake, and Josh. They provided me excellent advice and direction, but also gave me room to experiment, make decisions, and work through difficult problems independently. This research remains deeply interesting to me, and I’ll continue working on it alongside several independent and team projects that I hope to share soon.

What happens when a natural disaster destroys the infrastructure you need to call for help? California constantly faces the threat of earthquakes and wildfires. In 1906, the San Francisco earthquake ruptured nearly 300 miles of the San Andreas Fault. If a disaster of that scale struck today, buildings could collapse, power could disappear, and cellular and Wi-Fi networks could go dark. If you were trapped beneath rubble and your phone displayed “No Service,” how would you reach first responders? That question led to SafeRelay. Which I'm happy to share helped me and my teammates: Zhiyu Wen and Rishabh B. win 1st place in the Social Impact track at JacHacks SF last Sunday! SafeRelay turns ordinary smartphones into a peer-to-peer emergency communication network. A survivor creates a distress packet containing their location, condition, and request for help. The packet then travels between nearby phones over Bluetooth Low Energy. Each device stores the message and relays it forward without requiring cellular service or Wi-Fi. Even if none of the nearby phones are connected to the internet, the packet continues hopping from device to device. The first phone that eventually reaches any form of internet connectivity uploads the message chain to our server. From there, our Jac-powered operations console allows first responders to: • View off-grid emergency reports on a map • Understand a survivor’s location and situation • Prioritize incidents based on urgency • Compare incoming reports with live USGS and NWS hazard data We also integrated on-device AI using Apple’s Foundation Models framework. During an emergency, fear and stress can make it difficult to think clearly. Because the model runs directly on the phone, a survivor can describe their situation and receive survival tips even when the cloud is completely unreachable. It is not a replacement for professional emergency guidance, but it brings useful intelligence to the exact moment when connectivity and clear thinking may both be unavailable. We used Capacitor for the mobile shell and CoreBluetooth for the native iOS radio bridge, the part that could only be properly tested using physical phones. Thank you to Jason Mars , Vatsal Shah , Lingjia Tang , the entire JacHacks team, and Jaseci Labs for creating such an incredible event and technology. Also, thank you to Founders, Inc. for a wonderful place to hack and build our idea. Demo: https://lnkd.in/gvENDFkw Repository: https://lnkd.in/gH4hxhji #JacHacks #SocialImpact #EmergencyTechnology #OnDeviceAI #Bluetooth

One thing I am learning while trying to get Deadlink into real pilots: a yes is not the same thing as a path to yes. Someone can like the idea. They can say the problem is real. They can even want the demo. But if the next step needs 5 people, 3 approvals, a procurement process, and a budget cycle, that is not the same as "we can try this next week." I used to think pricing was mostly: "what is this worth?" Now I think early pricing is also: "what can this person actually approve without turning it into a whole process?" That sounds boring. It is not. For a startup, the difference between useful and buyable is massive. Especially in public safety / drones, where people are busy, budgets are weird, and nobody wants to add another tool unless it clearly solves a painful thing. So I am trying to get better at asking the real question earlier. Not just: "do you want this?" But: "what would make this easy to actually try?" Very unglamorous lesson. Probably one of the most useful ones so far. For people who have sold pilots into gov, public safety, healthcare, logistics, or any ops-heavy market: what made your first pilot actually buyable?

Over the last 9 months, I had the opportunity to work as a Quantitative Developer at QuantConnect . Before joining the team, I had competed in the QuantConnect Open Quant League, an international algorithmic trading competition featuring 20+ universities, securing 2x first place wins with the Triton Quantitative Trading (TQT) team at UC San Diego. At QuantConnect, I had the chance to work across many areas of quantitative finance and engineering, from quantitative development and research to machine learning engineering and AI orchestration. Some of my (open-source) contributions include: • Helping publish 200+ algorithmic trading strategies across multiple asset classes including: Equities, Equity Options, Crypto, Futures, and Forex • Improving our AI orchestration framework to enhance LLM-driven automations • Contributing to the launch of the Strategy Explorer platform • Extending futures contract support, improving our portfolio optimizers, integrating new datasets, and contributing other features to the LEAN Engine • Authoring technical examples and documentation to improve the developer experience Parallel to my work at QuantConnect, I mentored students through the full quantitative research lifecycle and published articles on novel methodologies on the QuantConnect Research platform. I also helped lead CSE 198: Introduction to Quantitative Finance at UC San Diego, building curriculum that introduced students to quantitative research and algorithmic trading using the QuantConnect framework. I'm incredibly grateful to the QuantConnect team for their mentorship and encouragement, especially Jared Broad and Derek Melchin for giving me the opportunity to join the team. Contributing to such an innovative and radically open-source project while seeing so many students adopt the QuantConnect framework has been one of the most meaningful experiences of my undergraduate career. All while also being a full-time student (for most of the time) :)
